plan.title: Why a too-high learning rate makes gradient descent diverge
plan.description: A ball sits on a stretched bowl-shaped loss surface. The bowl is gentle in one direction and steep in the other. Each step, the ball moves against the slope by the learning rate times the slope, leaves a trail and shows an arrow for its next move. With a small learning rate, the trail curves down to the bottom. Just above a threshold, it zigzags across the steep direction, landing higher each time, until it runs off the surface.
plan.reason: Divergence is easiest to see when you set the learning rate yourself, go step by step, and watch each jump overshoot the bottom and land higher than the last. Changing the steepness shows that "too high" depends on how curved the surface is.
interactions: Press play to let the host take one gradient step after another, or use Step once to move a single step and study it.
Move the learning rate below or above the threshold readout, then use Restart run, which keeps your settings, to compare a run that reaches the bottom with one that blows up.
Change the steepness and watch the threshold move: a steeper bowl tolerates only a smaller learning rate.
Orbit the camera to look along the steep direction, where the zigzag grows.
assumptions: Illustration: a simple made-up bowl-shaped loss, not a real model being trained.
The loss is 0.5 × (x² + steepness × y²), so its slope is (x, steepness × y), and each step is: new position = position − learning rate × slope.

Each step multiplies the steep-direction distance from the bottom by (1 − learning rate × steepness), and the gentle-direction distance by (1 − learning rate). If a multiplier's size exceeds 1, that distance grows. Exact for this bowl; only approximate near the bottom of real losses.

Readouts show the step number, the current loss, the steep-direction multiplier and the threshold of 2 ÷ steepness. A learning rate above the threshold diverges, and one exactly at it bounces back and forth forever.
The arrow at the ball shows the next step, which points against the slope (downhill direction scaled by the learning rate), not the slope itself.

Every run starts from the same point. It stops when the loss falls below 0.001 (converged), when the ball leaves the drawn surface, which covers −3 to 3 in each direction (diverged), or after 40 steps.
Heights are drawn scaled down so the whole bowl fits on screen. The loss readout shows the true value.
limitations: Real loss surfaces are not perfect bowls, so their divergence threshold is not exactly 2 ÷ curvature and can change during training.
There is no noise from mini-batches and no momentum or adaptive optimizer, only plain gradient descent.
Once the ball leaves the drawn surface, the scene shows it as diverged instead of following it further.
plan.learningGoal: Gradient descent diverges when the learning rate times the surface's curvature exceeds 2: each step overshoots the bottom by more than it started, so the loss grows instead of shrinking.

draft.title: Why a too-high learning rate makes gradient descent diverge
draft.description: A stretched bowl-shaped loss surface, steep from left to right and gentle from front to back. A red ball starts near the front edge. Each step it moves against the slope by the learning rate times the slope, leaving an orange trail, with a purple arrow showing its next step. Below the threshold the trail curves down to the bottom; above it the ball zigzags left and right, landing higher each time, until it leaves the surface.
assumptions: Illustration: a simple made-up bowl-shaped loss, not a real model being trained.
Loss = 0.5 × (gentle² + steepness × steep²); the steep direction runs left to right. Each step: new position = position − learning rate × slope.

Each step multiplies the steep distance from the bottom by (1 − learning rate × steepness) and the gentle distance by (1 − learning rate). A multiplier bigger than 1 in size makes that distance grow. Exact for this bowl; only approximate for real losses.

Threshold = 2 ÷ steepness: above it the run diverges; exactly at it the ball bounces back and forth forever. Every run starts at the same point; it stops at loss < 0.001 (converged), off the surface (−3 to 3, diverged) or after 40 steps.
The purple arrow is the next step (against the slope), drawn at 0.5 times its true length for every step, not the slope itself. Run takes 3 steps per second.

Heights are drawn at 0.06 × the loss, shaped for steepness 4; other steepness values stretch the whole surface vertically, so the gentle direction's drawn height is only approximate. The loss readout is exact.

findings.message: These captures never sample the default learning rate of 0.55. That run has a multiplier of -1.2 and should leave the surface after about 9 steps of zigzag. Restarting while keeping the old path, a learning rate exactly at the threshold, and steepness values other than 4 are not sampled either.

Near convergence the next-step arrow is drawn at half its true length, so it shrinks to a stub hidden inside the ball and its 'Next step' label is not readable. That is honest to the scale, but a learner cannot see the arrow here.

At learning rate 1 the host pins the diverged ball at height 2.7, but the bowl's edge there is at 2.16 and the trail ends at the edge. In the default view the ball floats in the air, apart from the end of its trail. The scene could fix this by clamping the ball's drawn position the same way it clamps the trail points, so the ball sits where the trail ends.
The first trail segment looks much thinner than the second, close to a hairline, in the default view.
At the high end the run diverges in only 2 steps, so the 'landing higher each time' zigzag is barely shown. The default of 0.55, which should show it clearly, is not sampled.
In the side view the host-clamped ball sits just past the end of the trail, which stops at the bowl's edge. It is less noticeable from this angle.

blocks.text:
Five captures pass and v0-s2 fails visually. The formulas and readouts are correct in every trace, but at the high end of the learning rate the default view shows the ball floating in the air away from the bowl.

- **Readout check:** the start loss of 3.14 and the step-8 loss of 0.0454 at learning rate 0.22 match the formula. So does the divergence in two steps to a loss of 58.32 at learning rate 1.
- **v0-s2 fault:** the host pins the ball at a drawn height of 2.7, but the bowl's edge there is at 2.16 and the orange trail ends at the edge. The scene could fix this by clamping the ball the same way it already clamps the trail.
- **Not sampled:** the default learning rate of 0.55, the restart that keeps the old path, the learning rate exactly at the threshold, and any steepness other than 4. Of these, 0.55 is the run that should show the slow zigzag up the bowl.
